summary.text: The immune system is a network of biological systems that protects an organism from diseases.
It detects pathogens such as viruses, bacteria, and parasites, along with cancer cells and foreign objects, and tells them apart from the organism's own healthy tissue.
Its defenses are layered: physical barriers first, then the innate response, then in vertebrates the adaptive system, which keeps a memory of pathogens it has met.

facts.label: Two subsystems
facts.value: The innate and the adaptive immune systems

facts.label: Adaptive memory
facts.value: Allows faster and stronger attacks on repeat encounters

facts.label: Antigens
facts.value: Substances that bind immune receptors and trigger a response

items.prompt: A bacterium slips past the skin and the body reacts at once, but with a general response not aimed at that exact germ. Which defense is this?

options.label: The innate immune system
The adaptive immune system
The physical barriers
Immunodeficiency

items.explain: If a pathogen breaches the barriers, the innate immune system provides an immediate but non-specific response.

items.prompt: Someone recovers from a virus. Months later the same virus returns and the body hits it faster and harder. What explains this?

options.label: The skin barrier grew thicker after the first infection
The virus weakened itself over time
The adaptive system kept its improved response as a memory
The body forgot the virus and started fresh

items.explain: The improved response is retained after the pathogen is gone as immunological memory, which allows faster and stronger attacks on later encounters.

items.prompt: A person's hyperactive immune system attacks their own thyroid as if it were a foreign invader. What is this called?

options.label: Immunodeficiency
Vaccination
Phagocytosis
Autoimmunity

items.explain: Autoimmunity results from a hyperactive immune system attacking normal tissues as if they were foreign organisms; Hashimoto's thyroiditis is one example.

items.prompt: A patient with HIV/AIDS has repeated, life-threatening infections. What is going on in their immune system?

options.label: It is less active than normal
It is hyperactive and attacking healthy tissue
It is working normally but has met too many pathogens
It is unable to produce any kind of barrier

items.explain: Immunodeficiency occurs when the immune system is less active than normal, which can result from conditions such as HIV/AIDS.

items.prompt: Why does a healthy immune system not normally attack the body's own tissue?

options.label: It only attacks things that are moving
It can tell the body's own molecules from foreign ones
It only attacks after a vaccination
It cannot reach tissue inside the body

items.explain: Both innate and adaptive immunity depend on distinguishing self from non-self molecules.

options.label: A cell that produces white blood cells in bone marrow
A barrier of skin and mucus that blocks germs
A substance that binds specific immune receptors and triggers a response
A medicine that suppresses the immune system

items.explain: Antigens are defined as substances that bind to specific immune receptors and elicit an immune response.
